A Storytelling Game to Foster Empathy and
Connect Emotionally with Breast Cancer Journeys
Jonas de Ara´ujo Luz Junior
PPGIA (CCT)
Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR)
Fortaleza-CE, Brasil
jonasluz@gmail.com
Maria Andr´eia Formico Rodrigues
PPGIA (CCT)
Universidade de Fortaleza (UNIFOR)
Fortaleza-CE, Brasil
andreia.formico@gmail.com
Jessica Hammer
HCI Institute/Entertainment Technology Center
Carnegie Mellon University (CMU)
Pittsburgh-PA, United States of America
hammerj@andrew.cmu.edu
Abstract—This work presents a storytelling prototype game to
foster empathy and connect people emotionally with breast can-\ncer journeys based on true real-world stories. We planned each
event to introduce different character’s possible choices, including
personal conﬂicts and doubts. This way, the players can have a
chance to experience the increasing sadness, desperation, etc., in
the patient character. Along with the narrative, we included 3D
body and facial animations to help build empathy and provide a
more engaging game experience. Although characters in 3D feel
alive, their animations require much more attention to anatomical
modeling, rigging, rendering, and camera control. We conducted
playtesting sessions. The results showed that the breast cancer
theme, animations, and the original game’s story pleased and
provoked an emotional and empathetic response in the players.
Index Terms—storytelling game, 3D animations, empathy,
breast cancer
I. INTRODUCTION
At a global level, cancer is a signiﬁcant disease burden that
continues to grow, exerting tremendous physical, emotional,
and ﬁnancial strain on individuals, families, communities, and
health systems [1]. Within this context, breast cancer is the
top cancer in women both in the developed and the developing
world. Although each breast cancer journey is different, very
commonly, the person’s emotions, physical conditions, and
mood can change due to a cancer diagnosis or due to the side
effects of treatment [2]. No one can predict for sure the side
effects or problems your loved one will have during the breast
cancer journey. And even after successful treatment, there is
still the chance that cancer will come back in the future. Thus,
learning to live with uncertainty is part of learning to live with
cancer, both for patients and people around them [3].
People have expectations for how breast cancer patients
should react to their diagnosis and types of treatment. These
expectations do not match the reality and make life harder for
the cancer patient. Caregivers and community members need
to connect with the real-life, complicated experience rather
than their imagined experience. People who may someday get
cancer also will beneﬁt from seeing the complexity of cancer,
so they are not surprised by it.
Empathy games can help with this problem by providing
situated experiences that players would not usually experience
to connect people emotionally with breast cancer journeys.

More precisely, empathy games aim to immerse the player
in a particular experience and empathize with the game’s
subject matter or protagonist through the experience of un-\nderstanding another person’s condition from their perspec-\ntive [4]. Although for many people games are only a form
of entertainment, empathy games can help put oneself into
these situations and understand how other people see the
world, make decisions, react to problems, as well as the
motivations and reasons why they behave, feel, and think
[5]. Often, empathy games are based on personal stories that
have touched and shaped the designers’ lives, making them
fascinating alternatives to explore dialogue around complex
feelings. Regarding this, storytelling is not only a successful
remote method of creating empathy but has been an engine of
social/cultural liberalization and change [6].
We argue that game design can be a powerful way in story-\ntelling games to connect with breast cancer patients and better
understand their journeys (from diagnosis through survivor-\nship) and their feelings, personal decisions, and consequences.
This work presents Cancer Sucks – Together for a Cause,
a storytelling game as a ﬁrst step to fostering empathy and
connecting people emotionally with breast cancer journeys.
II. RELATED WORK
Recently, a new generation of digital games is confronting
players with signiﬁcant human issues through interactive sto-\nrytelling to foster empathy, focusing on: mental disorders,
chronic diseases, health care, maltreatment on the grounds of
race, ethnicity, religion, ﬁnancial status, disability, or sexuality,
etc. [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. The success of these games
resides in the intersection of meaningful stories with game
design and how the balance between both is weighted.
Empathy Games – Empathy games affect players’ behavior
emotionally when observing the experiences of characters.
Indygo [13] is an interactive 2D game made with point ’n’
click elements set in a painting workshop. It tells the story of
a painter who locked himself out of the world, attempting to
illustrate what people affected by mood disorders may experi-\nence. Another 2D Empathy game is Papers, Please [9], which
is focused on human dramas experienced by immigrants,
having to judge whether or not they can enter the country.



The game stands out for its capacity to involve the player
in the intrigued political and social plot and for encouraging
players’ empathy. Aiming at helping people understand and
ﬁght against economic inequality, the game Spent [10] is about
surviving poverty and homelessness. The main mechanic in
the game is making choices. It presents in-game pop-up hints
and some summative textual data for further investigation and
discussion, with graphics represented as minimalist icons. It
focuses on ﬁnancial responsibility and exposes the difﬁculty
of human survival, hoping to touch the player empathetically.
Cancer Games – Most Cancer games are designed to improve
outcomes for cancer patients directly. Some examples are Re-\nMission [14] and its follow-up, Re-Mission 2 [8], in which
players are put inside the body of a ﬁctional cancer patient
with weapons like chemotherapy, antibiotics, and the body’s
natural defenses. CancerSpace [15] is a training game in the
cancer domain that presents the players with real-world cancer
situations (breast, cervical, and colon cancers). The interaction
involves a simulation of a cancer problem and decision-\nmaking. It uses animated avatars as characters, with a visual
aesthetic that still refers to Cartoon games. The avatars are
superimposed over still images of actual clinics to create the
game base, presenting most information in text format. Other
examples, also in 2D, are game-based learning applications
for health professionals working in cancer care [11] and
games based on decision-making and simulation of medical
procedures for cancer treatment [12]. A few games explore
the experience of having cancer. One well-known example is
That Dragon, Cancer [7], a 3D game that shares the story of
a small child diagnosed with a brain tumor and his journey
against terminal cancer, addressing this complex theme in a
poetic, intense and engaging way. The gap remaining is a lack
of prior research studies on the realistic stories of breast cancer
journeys, exposing the pain, drama, and dilemmas experienced
by patients, when essential decisions and priorities need to be
articulated and the treatment choices’ implications need to be
clearly understood by the patients and their families.
Visual Novels – A sub-genre of interactive narratives where
users can create or impact a storyline through certain actions
[16]. An example of a 2D computer game on the form of a
visual novel is The Time Mage, which was designed to promote
patient empowerment [17]. Basically, the players interact with
non-player characters in a virtual hospital environment to help
a patient character recover from a heart attack, having static
images and animations to help players better visualize the story
being told. Lastly, inspired by the Trauma Center series and
Life Signs, RavenHeart Hospital [18] is a medical visual novel
and 2D adventure game in which the player takes the role of an
ace surgeon, operating on patients with a variety of conditions.
While there have been many successful empathy games
and visual novels, games for cancer have primarily focused
on improving treatment outcomes. The only major empathy
game for cancer, That Dragon, Cancer [7], focuses on the
point of view of someone supporting a cancer patient, not
the patients themselves. This paper, therefore, ﬁlls a gap by
focusing on the breast cancer patient’s perspective and how
to deal with treatment options. Additionally, the goals of
this game mean that we want the player to understand the
character’s emotions and treat them as valid, regardless of
whether they share them. As a strategy to achieve this, we use
high visual realism to convey the character’s emotions. From
the gamer’s perspective, visual realism does not necessarily
come with a great gaming experience. However, the game’s
visual can attract the player’s eye and makes up its appeal,
a concept in Animation [19], creating a connection between
the story and the players. This strategy contrasts with the
low-ﬁdelity designs of existing empathy and cancer games
(Papers, Please [9], Spent [10], Indygo [13], and That Dragon,
Cancer [7]). Finally, the study of the emotions perceived in
the game characters, external to the player, and whether the
players themselves feel that emotions are also a remaining gap
relevant to provide an empathetic player experience.
III. DESIGN GOALS
Game designers are not storytellers but narrative architects
[20]. As narrative architects, we cannot control what players
feel, but we can create situations where they are likely to
feel them. Overall, our goal is to create an interactive breast
cancer experience ultimately designed to shed light on an
otherwise isolating experience to connect people with the real-\nlife, complicated experience and not their Imaginary. For this
game, we split up our design goal into smaller goals as follows:
Goal 1: To provide a cancer experience that evokes an emo-\ntional response from the player and that allows empathizing
with the game’s subject matter; Goal 2: To evoke empathy
through the breast cancer patient’s character design, including
dialogues, soundtrack, and facial & body expressions with
3D animations; Goal 3: To model diversity of emotions
(happiness, attentiveness, fear, sadness, desperation, distress,
insecurity, less stress, and resignation), and identify how many
and which of them the average player reports; Goal 4: To
foster immersion, and emotions that are not part of the “pretty”
breast cancer story (especially as they change over time and
do not ﬁt convenient narratives) to help explain why focusing
on some emotions over others and, thus, tell the story in a
better and more empathetic way; and Goal 5: To cleanly
separate player emotion (to evaluate whether the participants
were able to put themselves in the character’s shoes) and
character emotion (to improve empathy with characters and
engaging players with the storytelling).
IV. GAME DESCRIPTION
Cancer Sucks game follows a more realistic style, both
visual and true story-driven. It is based on a real-life personal
experience written by one of the game designers of this work
with informed consent to be used therein. Two characters are
the center point of the story: the cancer patient (female) and
the Oncologist (male). The focus of the narrative is to build up
breast cancer issues based on true real-world stories. Everyone
copes with a diagnosis of breast cancer in different ways,

experiencing a wide range of emotions. How to handle these
emotions and treatment choices involves complex decisions.
The storytelling takes place in a 3D medical clinic. For this
paper, we focus on the scene that happens in the oncologist’s
ofﬁce. We planned each new event to introduce different
character’s possible choices, including personal conﬂicts and
doubts. This way, the players can build up a breast cancer
problem together and have a chance to experience the increas-\ning sadness, desperation, etc., in the main female character,
on putting themselves in the character’s shoes. Fig. 1 displays
shots of some excerpts of the Cancer Sucks game.
This game scene in the doctor’s ofﬁce includes the following
series of actions: (1) Introducing the patient; (2) Telling the
breast cancer story showing how breast cancer is usually
diagnosed; (3) Posing a question to the player; (4) Showing the
consequences of possible different choices; and (5) Adjusting
feelings, life and initiatives for cancer treatment.
The whole story has several branchings. Thus the player
will need to play the game more than once to see the story
completely unfold. The player actions have consequences that
are reﬂected both in the narrative and in the characters’ anima-\ntions. In this work, we focus on the game scene that presents
an inconclusive diagnosis followed by the dilemma of making
the optimal breast biopsy decision based on mammographic
features, family medical history, and age. As a potential biopsy
patient, everyone has a choice in the procedure, and it is always
important to weigh up the different procedures available and
their consequences. With this in mind, the camera navigates
as a sequence of images in which the characters’ dialogue is
superimposed, allowing the player to interact through decision-\nmaking in the role of the patient’s character.
V. GAME ART & DESIGN
The choice of this genre for our game is based on the
following two premises: (1) Focus on the breast cancer story,
favoring the player’s involvement in the narrative context of
the game to foster empathy, and (2) Clear separation of the
game narrative layer (textual content) from its visual and
sound elements, allowing the use of artistic elements, such
as characters, scenarios, facial & body animations, music &
sound effects, which altogether compose the narrative.
Meaningful choices during gameplay and bringing a human
element into the story are the key differences in transforming
play into roleplay [21]. One of the ﬁrst steps after being told
someone has breast cancer will be learning about the medical
diagnosis and the possible treatment options. This initiative
helps to understand the disease process and get an idea of what
lies ahead. From that perspective, the awareness of available
choices and their consequences along the cancer journey helps
the audience of this game (patients, friends, family members,
and even professionals working in breast cancer care) to
understand better how stories and personal experiences are
woven throughout human lives, in varied contexts.
A foundational principle of visual storytelling is guiding the
viewer’s attention and, in the context of interactive storytelling
for games, using a player-centered approach [22]. Thus, we
begin creating the narrative shot list and deciding what the
characters would be and their relative positions in the 3D game
scene. Camera focus was another issue, and moving the focus
between the two characters was the chosen option.
Following the creation of the narrative, we designed a visual
composition to meet the concept of a playable, engaging,
and empathetic user’s experience focused on representing the
game’s theme in the most delicate way possible. The more
senses stimulated, the more people will relate to the story and
be moved by it. Thus, we have used the visual narrative script
to choose the musical theme, Feelings of Twilight Loop [23].
The aesthetic chosen for the game seeks to present the two
main subjects (patient and Oncologist) and game environment
(the doctor’s ofﬁce) as they would look in real life, aiming
to portray the scene more realistically. To achieve this goal,
we sought a collection of high-quality game assets from third
parties, with priority given to those with the free license: we
obtained the game environment, props, GUI elements, and
screen templates from the Unity Asset Store and downloaded
the soundtrack [23] & sound effects from freesound.org.
Cancer Sucks was designed to be a short visual novel,
using dynamic 3D images associated with textual narratives
favoring the dialogues between the two characters and the
player, whose interaction happens through options presented
in-game menus during the narrative. There will be a branching
tree of possibilities in the whole story, which will allow players
to take a variety of different paths through the plot, depending
on what choices they make at the predeﬁned narrative points
that correspond to a branch. Although the story is explorable,
there is only a single beginning and end in this scene in the
doctor’s ofﬁce, with events traversed in more than one order,
depending on the player’s choice.
VI. GAME DEVELOPMENT
The design goals, presented in Section III to increase
empathy, guided speciﬁc art & game design choices and how



to implement them. Cancer Sucks game has been developed
with Unity 3D engine (which made it possible to generate a
multiplatform game, which runs also on both personal comput-\ners and mobile devices), and we wrote its interactive narrative
in Ink, an open-source scripting language. In addition, Adobe
Fuse CC and Mixamo.com were used, respectively, to create
and animate the main game characters.
A. Narrative Presentation
When playing a storytelling game, the storyline may seem
like a linear story. However, this is rarely the case since
the storyline changes over time, especially when it does
not ﬁt convenient narratives. In our game, the exchange of
information between oncologists and patient is essential to
good decision-making. As in real life, serious consequences
can result if the patients are not listened to or are not given
the information, time, and support they need to make personal
decisions about their cancer journey.
The narrative ﬂow of our game is shown in Fig. 2. In this
particular shot scene, there are three branching scenarios where
the player learns about the pros and cons of each biopsy
procedure to be aware of which one to choose as the story
evolves. Regarding the nodes shown in the ﬂow diagram,
they have been implemented by editing one or more timelines
synchronized with the narrative of the Ink script. As usually
happens in games of the visual novel genre, the Cancer Sucks
narrative is represented by its visual and dynamic elements
(animated 3D scenes), as well as by its textual narrative. The
latter is displayed at the bottom of the interface, with most
screens dedicated to the animated scenes and options menus.
B. Characters’ Animations
Characters are the most challenging aspect of animation,
as each part of their bodies must act independently. Thus,
facial and body pose changes of the game characters have
been treated as separate entities. We included the animations
and the narrative to help build more empathy toward the patient
and provide a more engaging experience. Although characters
in 3D feel alive, their animations require much more attention
to modeling, rigging, anatomical reﬁnements, rendering, and
camera control. We created the custom characters in Adobe
Fuse CC and then rigged and animated them in Mixamo.com,
also from Adobe. We chose these tools because they are free
of cost and offer seamless integration, favoring the automatic
generation of the characters’ facial blend shapes [24].
In our game, the character’s facial expressions and body
animations of the patient are modeled in such a way to possibly
cue the audience about her emotions and bring up a range of
intense feelings also in the player, which people are not used to
dealing with daily. Thus, based on a true story, we initially did
a detailed study to understand what expressions would create
facial appeal by internalizing and representing the diversity
of emotions that the female character felt during the medical
appointment, especially from the moment the doctor says the
mammogram result is inconclusive. Anyone who has had this

All facial animations have been implemented directly in
the Animation and Timeline editors for Unity 3D by creating
reusable clips and animation for generating lip movements and
blinking eyes. The mixing of blend shapes to represent facial
variations as combinations of several given shapes can produce
natural-looking results (Fig. 3). Camera movements have been

The synchronism between timelines and narrative texts
happens on the side of the timelines, through the emission
of signals at synchronization’s moments, by indicating when
a piece of text is displayed. And, on the side of the Ink script
execution mechanism, by marking with a tag the narrative
moment, we should execute a timeline. Additionally, to facil-\nitate the generation of varied emotions from facial poses and
feed the game’s animations, we have implemented a prototype
tool for visualizing the facial poses, with transition dials
between feelings of the same nature, inspired by commercial
3D animation tools, such as Daz3D and Poser.
VII. PLAYTESTING
This section describes how we used playtesting to provide
feedback to the game designers and also understand and assess
the core elements of the overall gaming experience [25].
Each playtesting session was conducted remotely and lasted
approximately 15 minutes.
A. Participants
Internal and external playtesting provide different kinds of
value to a game design process - internal playtesters are experts
& close to the game, external playtesters are closer to eventual
players but less able to give expert advice.
The ﬁrst people who tested Cancer Sucks were the de-\nvelopers. Using internal playtest strategies, they played the
game prototype for an extended period to provide thoughtful
feedback, revise and test its functionalities [26]. With this
methodology, we ﬁnish one phase of playtesting and then start
the next, in which eighteen participants took part in the user
experience and usability tests. There were nine women and
nine men. The people who tested the game were coworkers
(7), medical doctors (2), colleagues (2), and graduate (5) and
postgraduate students (2). We divided the age group of the
participants as follows: eight between 21 and 30 and ten
between 33 and 59 years old. Two participants are breast
cancer survivors, eight have at least one immediate family
member who has been diagnosed with breast cancer, and
eleven playtesters who like to play video games. We then
followed the general methodology proposed by Moreno-Ger
et al. [27] to evaluate the game’s usability. The playtesters
were given brief instructions about the context of the game and
its mechanics and prompted to play it on their own, without
further instructions. We instructed the playtesters to speak out
loud while playing whenever they wanted to. The session was
recorded through Google Meet, simultaneously capturing both
the game screen and the user’s verbal and nonverbal reactions.
After the playtesting session, all playtesters completed a
questionnaire built-in Google Form.
B. Questionnaire
Table I shows the questionnaire in digital form we used
to evaluate the gaming experience, with a list of closed and
open questions. In addition, we added a short questionnaire
section to collect some user’s proﬁle data, such as name,
age, occupation, and three yes-no choices about whether the
participant: (1) is a breast cancer survivor, (2) identify oneself
as having close family members or friends who have or have
had breast cancer, and (3) likes to play video games or not.
Most of the items highlighted in blue in Table I are closed-\nended questions (Qs. 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6). Each item highlighted
in yellow (from Q9 to Q17) is rated with a 5-point Likert scale
(5 means they Strongly agree, 1 means they Strongly disagree).
The questionnaire also allows suggestions for reﬁnement and
improvements highlighted in pink (Q18), making the player’s
feedback particularly relevant for game development. Users
had to answer these questions remotely after playing the game,
and the results were then compared and analyzed.
VIII. RESULTS AND LESSONS LEARNED
We used our design goals to organize this section. Overall,
the playtest results helped ﬁnd failings and point out improve-\nment points to reﬁne the game experience, particularly related
to 3D animations. The overall impression of the playtesters,
including their ﬁrst game impression, was positive. They liked
the game’s story and recognized its logical and understandable
structure. Play-testers also evaluated the design aspects of the
game, such as visual aesthetics, sound effects, musical theme,

Regarding Goals 1 and 4, among the eighteen playtesters,
all reported having understood the story (Q1), and only one
was unable to put herself in the patient’s shoes (Q3): one of
the breast cancer survivors. When cancer affects a person’s
physical health, it may bring up a range of intense feelings
that one is not used to or is not comfortable dealing with.
Thus, how a person reacts to play a game about diagnosis and
treatment can depend on her cancer experience and personal
choices, among other factors. About Q2, in the blue-colored
region of Fig. 2, the order we presented the biopsy options
(FNA, CNB, and Surgical Biopsy) may have inﬂuenced the
playtesters’ behavior: thirteen of them (72,22%) have picked
the ﬁrst option (FNA). This may be due to primary bias,
because it was the ﬁrst choice they read or because they
were racing through the playtest. In future playtests, we plan
to randomize the order of the biopsy choices to observe the
consequences of this change in the participants’ experience.
Only one playtester (a 25-year-old female who likes to play
video games and has family members who have had breast
cancer) reported not having understood the initial reaction of
the patient (Q5) in the face of the inconclusive results shown
on the mammogram (Fig. 1.c). In particular, she criticized the
positioning of the narrative dialog box (displayed at the very
bottom of the game interface), regretting that, for many times,
it has stolen her attention from the characters’ animations.
Anyway, all participants were unanimous in understanding the
patient’s conﬂict in having to choose, among three unknown
procedures, the most suitable breast biopsy for her case (Q6).

Both the story of the game (Q14) and its gameplay
(Q15) pleased almost all participants (seventeen), with only
one playtester being indifferent (a 33-year-old female post-\ngraduate student who does not like to play video games
and has never had a close relative with breast cancer). Con-\ntrastingly, this particular playtester immediately put herself
in the patient’s shoes, trying but not succeeding, to avoid a
feeling of deep sadness. In Q18, this user explicitly stated that
she dislikes drama-type games based on real-life sad stories,
essentially because these game genres make her suffer. Most
playtesters (fourteen) said in Q16 that they felt immersed in the
story. Among the other four, two expressed indifference, and
two disagreed, reporting not having felt immersion. For some
of them, the immersion in the story was hindered mainly by
the facial animations of the doctor’s character. All participants
reported enjoying the experience and playing the game (Q17).
About Goals 3 and 5, the cancer context, original story,
melancholic soundtrack, and 3D models and animations jointly
played a crucial role in fostering empathy. These elements
also make it possible for most of the playtesters to identify
several emotions expressed by the patient (Fig. 5.a) and the
experience of emotions that sparked personal feelings during
gameplay (Fig. 5.b). Commonly, many women who have been
diagnosed with breast cancer feel a whole roller coaster of
emotions, including some of those modeled for our game (Fig.
3). On the positive side, almost all participants declared to
have felt emotions through the patient’s character. Regarding
those presented in Q7 and Q8, i.e., happiness, attention,
fear, sadness, despair, distress, insecurity, less suffering, and
resignation, Fig. 5.a shows a word cloud chart that highlights
the most frequent emotions visually perceived by playtesters
in the patient character, two of which, fear and insecurity



(Figs. 3.c and g, respectively) were recognized by all eighteen
participants, and one of them, distress (Fig. 3.f), by ﬁfteen.

Eleven playtesters were declared attentive, and eight per-\nceived attentiveness (Fig. 3.b) in the patient character. With
a focus on the patient’s emotional behavior, nine participants
recognized desperation (Fig. 3.e), and ﬁfteen noticed distress
(Fig. 3.f). Distress was also felt by nine while playing the
game. Their facial expressions changed. Three of them had
eyes well up with tears. As in real life, loved ones, friends,
doctors, and family members of cancer patients and survivors
commonly share some of the same patient’s feelings. Everyone
visually noticed fear (Fig. 3.c) and insecurity (Fig. 3.g) in
the patient’s actions. The former was also felt by two users,
whereas the latter by ﬁve. Very few playtesters felt or identiﬁed

perceived by thirteen playtesters in the patient’s emotional

players, establishing a clear connection of feelings merged.
No one felt or recognized happiness (Fig. 3.a) in the patient’s
facial expressions, and less stress (Fig. 3.h) was observed and
felt by very few users (22.22% and 11.11%, respectively).
Text is quite essential to storytelling-based games. Regard-\ning Goal 2, in Q9, all participants Strongly agreed that the
dialogue texts were easy to read and understand (Fig. 4).\nRegarding Q10, ﬁfteen playtesters felt that the melancholic
soundtrack and sound effects stimulated empathy. Among the
remaining users, two had Neutral opinions, and one Disagreed.\nThe playtester who disagreed made exciting suggestions on
how to bring each scene to life to provoke more empathy. For
example, to use the soundtrack to shape what is visually seen,
reinforcing dramatic developments and emotional reactions
through the soundtrack’s loudness and timbre variation. Facial
expression is an essential part of nonverbal communication.\nIn this regard, the playtesters’ responses were divided in Q11:\n50% found the character’s facial expressions believable, three
reported neutral opinions, and six disagreed. Perhaps we can
correlate this result to the suggestions made in Q18 of Table
I. Several participants said that the facial animations of the
doctor had very few visual variations, making it signiﬁcantly
more complex to connect emotionally with him. We agree
that we have not polished the doctor’s facial expressions as
much as those of the patient’s. We also reused some doctor’s
facial expressions in several parts of the game narrative, which
may have caused a certain discomfort in ﬁve playtesters, who
reported not being as realistic as they should be. Only one
male participant under the age of 30, a graduate student
who likes to play games and has close family members
who have had breast cancer, afﬁrmed not having experienced
feelings of empathy for the patient (Q4), ﬁnding this character
more like a cartoon-style 3D model. Even so, this playtester
visually recognized certain patient’s emotions (Q7), such as
insecurity, fear, distress, desperation, and sadness, as well
as felt distressed and insecure playing the game (Q8). But,
regardless, this user made it clear that he was indeed moved
by the original story and melancholic soundtrack of the game.\nOn the other hand, in the responses to Q12, most playtesters
(ﬁfteen) agreed that the body animations of the two characters
were believable, with only two having chosen “neutral” and
one “disagree”, which conﬁrms that the use of ready-made
animations adjusted according to the characters and selected
in Mixamo.com was an appropriate project decision. Fourteen
playtesters liked the visual aesthetics (Q13). The remaining
four participants were indifferent.
Finally, regarding the lessons learned, the player experience
and feedback on a narrative game is hard to measure, mainly
because empathy is subjective and difﬁcult to evaluate within
the conﬁnes of a game [28]. As the game evolves with more
scenes and narratives, it is why the players’ choices along
the way create the journey. As the player travels through the
story, one may develop a relationship with the game characters
along the way. The playtesting sessions helped identify the
main issues that participants brought to light and prioritize
the next steps for evolving our game. To name some of
them: (1) aesthetics and emotional expressions matter, (2)\nrealistic character’s emotions may create strong ties with the
game (players need to empathize with some character or
aspect of the game), and (3) multiple playtesters are crucial
to understanding the behavior of the audience, that is, it is
essential to get a variety of different players to maximize the
identiﬁcation of potential game problems and needs.
IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
Storytelling games in the health area pose critical human
elements of a story to players, then give meaningful choices to
solve them. This work presented a storytelling prototype game
to foster empathy and connect people emotionally with breast
cancer journeys. We began by designing a player experience
focused on the lived experience story of a woman who has
been diagnosed, treated, and is currently a cancer-free survivor.\nWe reinforce that storytelling games may offer, through differ-\nent narratives, a range of breast cancer scenarios that can be
shared with a larger audience as an innovative resource to help
patients, family members, friends, and health professionals
understand the patient’s priorities and preferences to deliver
genuine patient-centric care. This work showed it, with one
particular breast cancer experience in depth. Also, we have
implemented a visualization tool to help calibrate the poses
for the character’s facial expressions.
Although the number of participants of the playtesting study
was limited, the results showed that the breast cancer theme



and the original game’s story pleased and provoked an emo-\ntional and empathetic response. However, more playtesting
data is still necessary to evaluate whether the 3D realistic
human ﬁgures of Cancer Sucks can foster empathy and create
emotional connections or risk making real humans uncomfort-\nable due to a possible “Uncanny Valley” effect [29].
Playtesters who like to play video games have offered
more technical feedback, particularly about the characters’
facial and body animations, motivating us to plan future
game improvements. Three-dimensional character animation
is not an easy task to master [30]. The more complex the
character is, the more reﬁned skill is required to convey realism
in every scene detail (facial expressions, body movements,
illumination, camera angle, action, direction, motion, etc.).
As future work, further analysis and synthesis are needed to
develop immersive narrative experiences capable of fostering
empathy and connecting people emotionally with breast cancer
journeys. Also, interaction can be extremely useful to improve
player’s engagement and emotional connections with virtual
characters. Therefore, further experiments with more interac-\ntion options can be an interesting direction for future work.\nIn addition, the reﬁnement of our tool for facial animations is
foreseen, in such a way as to evolve into a facial expression
editor, which we can use for recording the emotions’ poses
and generating lipsync animations, with the narrative text as
input data. Some possible initiatives to improve the dynamism
of the scenes would include the use of more precise camera
movements. Some cutscenes focused only on some parts of
the characters’ bodies (for example, on the eyes, hands, etc.,
instead of focusing on the whole scene), the polishing of eyes
and mouth movements, and the inclusion of blend shapes in
the region of the characters’ forehead to generate wrinkles of
expression. We also plan to improve the soundtrack quality by
better representing the dramatic atmosphere of the narrative
with its ups and downs, varying according to the different
emotions expressed by the characters. Finally, further testing
is planned using the same textual narrative but replacing the
3D characters with 2D characters, to compare and evaluate the
results of this change in players’ feelings. We also expect to
continue conducting UX tests with other participants to collect
suggestions, criticisms, and recommendations to improve our
prototype game further.
